title: In 1994 we watched a comet, torn apart by Jupiter’s gravity, crash into it piece by piece

cover.alt: Hubble image of Jupiter’s cream and orange cloud bands, with a large dark brown blotch and ring near the top where a comet fragment struck.
cover.credit: Hubble Space Telescope Jupiter Imaging Team · Public domain

body: Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 was the first active comet ever seen orbiting a planet. On 7 July 1992 it passed just over 40,000 km above Jupiter’s cloud tops, and the planet’s tidal forces pulled it apart into a train of fragments up to 2 km across. Two years later, between 16 and 22 July 1994, the pieces slammed one after another into Jupiter’s southern hemisphere at about 60 km/s. It was **the first direct observation of two Solar System bodies colliding**, and the dark scars were more visible than the Great Red Spot for many months.

slides.question: How many separate impacts did astronomers see as the broken comet hit Jupiter?
slides.explanation: 21 distinct impacts were observed, over about a week in July 1994.

slides.alt: A long diagonal line of small glowing red blobs on black, each a fragment of the same comet.
slides.caption: Hubble’s view of the comet’s icy fragments strung out in a line, months before they hit Jupiter.
slides.credit: NASA, ESA, H. Weaver and E. Smith (STScI) · Public domain

slides.label: megatons of TNT: the estimated energy of the largest impact, by fragment G
slides.text: That is about 600 times the world’s nuclear arsenal. Even the first impact, fragment A, threw up a fireball plume more than 3,000 km high.

slides.heading: One fragment and the scar it left
slides.note: Fragments were up to 2 km across; the spot from fragment G was over 12,000 km wide

Carolyn and Eugene Shoemaker and David Levy discover it: comet Shoemaker–Levy 9

slides.question: The fragments struck the side of Jupiter facing away from Earth. What saw them hit as it happened?
slides.explanation: NASA’s Galileo spacecraft, then 1.6 astronomical units from Jupiter, was able to see the impacts as they occurred. The scars later became more visible than the Great Red Spot.
